title: Free-Energy Differences from Nonequilibrium Fluctuations in High Dissipation
abstract: Equilibrium free-energy differences can be measured from nonequilibrium work fluctuations using fluctuation theorems, such as the Jarzynski equality and the Crooks fluctuation theorem. However, these approaches become statistically inefficient in high-dissipation regimes because their convergence requires trajectories with negative entropy production, events that occur exponentially rarely. Here, we demonstrate that repeated measurements of trajectory fluctuations are sufficient to determine entropy production without relying on such rare events, or to determine a lower bound on it when only partial measurements are available. This information then yields exact estimates of free-energy differences, or rigorous bounds. We validate this approach, named EquiNET, with numerical simulations, including one of biomolecular folding and unfolding, showing that it recovers accurate free-energy estimates even in regimes where conventional approaches fail.
summary: This paper introduces EquiNET, a novel technique to calculate equilibrium free-energy differences from non-equilibrium work measurements. It overcomes the statistical limitations of traditional fluctuation theorems in highly dissipative systems by estimating entropy production directly from trajectory fluctuations. The method is validated on biomolecular folding, demonstrating accurate $\Delta F$ estimation where conventional methods fail.
main_problem: The primary challenge is accurately determining equilibrium free-energy differences ($\Delta F$) from non-equilibrium work fluctuations, especially in high-dissipation regimes where standard fluctuation theorems fail due to rare event sampling.
main_result: The proposed EquiNET method successfully estimates $\Delta F$ (or provides rigorous lower bounds) by utilizing trajectory fluctuations to estimate entropy production without relying on rare negative entropy production events.
method: The approach uses a variational optimization procedure derived from the short-time Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation (TUR) to infer the instantaneous entropy production rate ($\sigma(t)$) from the first two cumulants of a weighted stochastic current.
model_or_system: The theory is applied to general $d$-dimensional overdamped systems evolving under time-dependent protocols, validated numerically using biomolecular folding/unfolding simulations (polymer hairpin model).
key_observables: Work ($W$), Entropy Production ($\Delta S_{	ext{tot}}$), Free-energy difference ($\Delta F$), and the instantaneous entropy production rate ($\sigma(t)$).
important_parameters: High-dissipation regimes, temperature ($T$), and the structure of the time-dependent potential $\lambda(t)$.
main_assumptions: The method exploits the asymptotic behavior of entropy production fluctuations in the short-time limit, allowing the use of only the first two cumulants of the stochastic current.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the EquiNET framework, showing how integrating the inferred $\sigma(t)$ yields $\langle \Delta S_{	ext{tot}} angle$ and subsequently $\Delta F$, including visualizations for biomolecular folding.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem limitation, proposes the EquiNET method based on the TUR, details the variational inference procedure for $\sigma(t)$, and validates the approach using numerical simulations, including a detailed analysis of a polymer folding protocol.
why_interesting: This work provides a robust, data-driven methodology for calculating fundamental thermodynamic quantities ($\Delta F$) from noisy, non-equilibrium measurements, which is crucial for analyzing complex dynamics in molecular and condensed matter systems.
